Mask ventilation

Indications

Apnea or impending respiratory arrest (gasping)

Prior to intubation

Mask ventilation can be achieved with:

One provider: using BVM, one hand pressing the bag, the other one making a seal with the face

Two providers: using BVM, one dedicated to maintaining a tight seal while the second one is responsible provides just enough volume to raise the chest or

One provider and mechanical ventilator

Step 1: Patients should be placed in a sniffing or ramped position (head tilt/chin lift and/or jaw thrust), in trauma patients suspected for C spine injury, only jaw thrust is done

Step 2: Airway adjuncts should be placed (NPA and OPA if the patient doesn’t have gag reflex)

Step 3: Apply a properly fitted mask (covers mouth and nostrils without any gaps between the mask and face), there is adult and pediatric masks

Step 4: make a good seal between the mask and the face. A CE (anesthetist grip) grip can be used, if it is done by one hand and gripped from the side then the mask will tilt to one side allowing the air to leak under the opposite side

Step 5: Volume, Rate and pressure

Volume: previously volume per ventilation for adults was 800 ml but recent guidelines suggest a more conservative 6- 8 ml/kg per ventilation (same as the normal tidal volume) ( for an adult weighing 80kg approx. 480- 640 ml per ventilation) and even less for patients with known respiratory illness

Higher volume than 8 ml/kg would risk gastric insufflation and aspiration, also it leads to hypocapnia and barotrauma to lungs

In reality, metrics are not that useful because they will vary with each patient weight and lung capacity. So it is best to look for adequate chest rise and fall with each ventilation

Bag valve mask

BVM contain a self inflating bag, attached to a nonrebreathing valve and then to a face mask and an oxygen source which is attached to a reservoir bag

“A good seal”

If the mask gripped around the lower half of the face then it allows the air to escape through the nasal bridge

If the mask gripped with a rotated grip (rotated hold) then it provides better seal than both of the techniques mentioned already

If two providers are involved then mask ventilation will be more effective, one provider (the operator) can concentrate on their BVM technique while the second provider (the assistant) can use both hands to provide an effective mask seal one the patient face

For the assistant, two grips can be used:

CE grip

Thenar eminence grip (TE): it is achieved by using thenar muscles to place downward pressure one the mask while the four finger of each hand pullin the jaw upward

If you are unable to achieve a mask seal consider placing an extraglottic device if there is no gag reflex or other contraindications or endotracheal intubation

Rate

For patients in cardiac arrest, current UK and European guidelines recommend inflation duration of one second every 5 seconds resulting in a rate of one complete ventilation every 6 seconds or 10 ventilation in a minute

For patients breathing spontaneously then the normal resting minute ventilation in humans is around 70- 100 ml/kg/min and it achieved by delivering the normal tidal volume (6-8 ml/kg/ventilation) in a rate of 12- 16 breaths /min (same as normal respiratory rate)

Pressure

In BVM ventilation it is possible to over inflate the patient by squeezing the bag too hard or too fast or too much

Inspiratory pressure if exceeds 20 mmHg, this would increase the risk of forcing the air in the stomach (gastric insufflation) and spiration

Inspiratory pressures should be around 15 mmHg

BVM that are equipped with a pressure responsive, and flow limiting valves, reduces mean airway pressure thus reducing the risk for gastric insufflation compared to standard bags

PEEP

Positive end expiratory pressure may be used during BVM to improve oxygenation, PEEP keeps more alveoli open and prevents atelectasis thus improving oxygentation and it also prevent lung injury

PEEP should be used cautiously in hypotensive or heart failure patients

Difficult BVM

Characteristic of difficult BVM are collected in mnemonic MOANS

M Mask seal: facial hair or facial trauma can interfere in achieving adequate seal

O obesity/ obstruction: obesity means increased soft tissue in the airway and may cause further occlusion when the patient is AMS

A age: extremes of age can be difficult to ventilate due to anatomic changes

N no teeth: BVM in no teeth patient is ineffective

S snoring: snoring means that soft tissues (e.g. tongue) is occluding the airway and airway maneuvers and adjuncts are required

In difficult BVM , supraglottic airway or intubation is preferred

Complications

Mask ventilation may:

Accelerate hypoxia if not enough oxygen is provided

Accelerate hypercapnia if not enough CO2 is removed, leading to brain damage

Over ventilation can exacerbate existing lung injuries and lead to gastric insufflation and subsequently aspiration
